newsitem.title: USA: US lawmaker says Huang briefings put lives at risk.
newsitem.headline: US lawmaker says Huang briefings put lives at risk.

text.p: Intelligence briefings that former Democratic fund-raiser John Huang received when he was a Commerce Department official included information that could have led to the death of a CIA informant, the Washington Times reported in Tuesday editions.

Representative Gerald Solomon, the New York Republican who heads the U.S. House Rules Committee, which is investigating the 1996 campaign financing controversy, made the allegation in a letter to President Bill Clinton, the paper said.

He described the secret briefings given Huang, a former executive of the Indonesian financial conglomerate Lippo Group, as "extremely serious and dangerous," and asked Clinton to make White House officials who knew about the briefings available to congressional investors.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry declined all comment on the matter. "I'm not going to comment on something that involves intelligence briefings and that is being properly investigated," he told reporters at his midday briefing.

"The president believes very strongly that if anyone has broken the law they ought to be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law and that should be within the domain of those who investigate those kind of allegations," he added.
Congress and the Justice Department are investigating allegations that foreign countries may have sought to influence the 1996 presidential and congressional elections with campaign contributions.

"Even the hint that the lives of individuals who trusted our government have been put at risk moves the quest for the truth to the highest level," Solomon wrote in his letter, according to the newspaper report.

Solomon quoted testimony released during a civil suit filed by a conservative watchdog group, Judicial Watch, against the Commerce Department. In his testimony last week, CIA officer John Dickerson said Huang, a former Democratic National Committee fund-raiser, received three intelligence reports whose unauthorised release could result in the death of a source.
Dickerson, who briefed Huang 37 times, said he gave him "raw intelligence reports" about Asian countries, and Huang showed an interest in intelligence on China and Taiwan.
Solomon has previously charged that Huang passed classified data to Lippo.

The newspaper said that on two occasions, Huang received documents labeled "secret" followed by three telephone calls to Lippo Group, and on one occasion, he scheduled a meeting with Chinese officials.
